prompt.context: Our client is a non-profit organization whose mission is to bring better vision care and access to third world African countries. The organization currently only offers services in one country and provides vision care to 20,000 people a year through its three service locations. The non-profit has contacted Deloitte to develop a strategy to reach more of the population and cover operating expenses.
prompt.question: What are your recommendations for reaching more of the population and covering operating expenses?

clarifying_info.q: What is the total population for the country?
clarifying_info.a: Total population is 2M, which means a 1% penetration rate.
In the three largest city centers in the country, but the majority of the population lives in rural areas.

clarifying_info.q: How does the organization currently cover operating expenses?
clarifying_info.a: The eye health exams are free to anyone who visits a location. Revenue comes from the purchase of eye glasses (includes case, cleaning cloth, etc.). Each pair costs $150, which is 10x the daily income for the average person.

clarifying_info.q: How many people purchase eye glasses?
clarifying_info.a: 50% of the population served purchase glasses and report improved ability to earn a living.

clarifying_info.q: What are the penetration and financial goals?
clarifying_info.a: Reach as much of the population as possible and cover operating expenses.

clarifying_info.q: What are the operating expenses for the locations?
clarifying_info.a: Total operating expenses for the organization are $1.25M.

exhibits.title: World Vision — Package Options
exhibits.shows: Three tiered eye glass kit packages with price, cost, and percentage of sales for each tier (Premium, Standard, Basic)

Premium.includes: Second pair of sunglasses and better quality lenses

framework: Market Penetration: analyze barriers to awareness and access preventing the 99% of the population not currently served
Awareness & Education: assess whether the population understands the benefits of routine eye health exams
Access: majority of population lives in rural areas, far from the three city-center locations — travel time up to one day
Marketing channels: consider low literacy rates and limited media access; word-of-mouth may be most effective
Operating hours: ensure hours align with work schedules and daily routines of the target population
Financial Sustainability: calculate current revenue vs. operating expenses and determine what is needed to break even
Revenue: glasses kits at $150 each; 50% of 20,000 served buy glasses = 10,000 kits x ($150 - $50 cost) = $1M contribution
Budget deficit: -$250K; need to sell 2,500 additional kits to break even
Pricing: organization will not charge for exams; kit price already 10x average daily income — raising price is constrained
Cost cutting: no cost-cutting options available
Mission focus: non-profit goal is mission fulfillment (reach), not profit maximization

questions.prompt: Walk through the financial situation: what is the current budget deficit and how many additional glasses kits must be sold to break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate current revenue from kit sales, subtract operating expenses to find the deficit, then divide the deficit by the per-kit margin to find the additional units required.

math.setup: Contribution per kit = Price - Cost = $150 - $50 = $100. Kits sold = 20,000 people x 50% = 10,000. Total contribution = 10,000 x $100 = $1,000,000. Budget deficit = $1,000,000 - $1,250,000 = -$250,000. Additional kits needed = $250,000 / $100 per kit = 2,500 kits.
steps: Additional kits to break even: $250,000 / $100 = 2,500 kits
math.answer: Budget deficit is $250,000; need to sell 2,500 additional kits to cover operating expenses.

questions.prompt: Given the goal of expanding reach and the need to sell 2,500 additional kits, what are your marketing recommendations? (brainstorming)
questions.guidance: Candidate should address both increasing awareness/education and the practical constraints of operating in a developing country (low literacy, limited media, rural populations, income levels).

questions.prompt: World Vision is considering offering three tiered kit packages instead of the single standard kit. Review Exhibit 1 and assess the financial impact of moving to this package model.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate margin and total contribution for each tier using current 10,000 units sold, apply the sales-mix percentages, sum total contribution, and compare to the current $1M to determine whether the new model is better or worse financially.

math.setup: Use current 10,000 total units sold and apply the sales mix. Premium: 10% of 10,000 = 1,000 kits, margin = $350 - $250 = $100, contribution = $100,000. Standard: 30% of 10,000 = 3,000 kits, margin = $200 - $125 = $75, contribution = $225,000. Basic: 60% of 10,000 = 6,000 kits, margin = $150 - $50 = $100, contribution = $600,000. Total new contribution = $925,000. New deficit = $925,000 - $1,250,000 = -$325,000.
math.answer: Total contribution under the new package model is $925,000, resulting in a larger deficit of $325,000 vs. the current $250,000. The tiered model is financially worse due to higher costs on Premium and Standard kits.

brainstorming.prompt: Given the goal of expanding World Vision's reach and the need to sell an additional 2,500 pairs of glasses, what are your recommendations for marketing the service?

categories.name: Awareness & Education
ideas: Referral incentives to increase word-of-mouth advertising
Vision health ambassadors placed in rural communities
Pamphlets and portable speakers with audio messages for low-literacy populations
Community leader partnerships to spread the message locally

categories.name: Access & Outreach
ideas: Traveling clinic days where optometrists go to rural communities instead of waiting in city locations
Mobile service units that rotate through villages on a set schedule
Partnerships with local organizations (churches, NGOs, schools) to host pop-up clinics

categories.name: Scheduling & Convenience
ideas: Adjust operating hours to align with work schedules and market days in rural areas
Offer weekend or evening clinics to reduce lost income for visitors

categories.name: Pricing & Incentives
ideas: Volume discounts for families purchasing multiple kits
Subsidized or installment payment options to address the affordability barrier (kit = 10x daily income)
Donor-funded voucher programs to cover kit cost for the poorest patients

recommendation: World Vision should retain the Basic kit as its sole offering rather than adopting the tiered package model, which would increase the deficit from $250K to $325K
Focus on closing the $250K gap by selling 2,500 additional kits through expanded outreach — this is achievable given the enormous untapped market (99% of the 2M population)
Prioritize rural access through traveling clinic days and community health ambassadors to address the primary barrier of geographic distance
Invest in word-of-mouth and audio-based marketing given low literacy and limited media access in target communities
risks: Traveling clinics and ambassador programs increase operating costs, potentially widening the deficit before additional kit sales materialize
Affordability remains a structural barrier — at 10x daily income, voluntary purchase rates may not improve without subsidy or donor support
Organizational capacity may be insufficient to rapidly scale from 20,000 to meaningfully higher patient volumes
next_steps: Pilot a traveling clinic program in one rural region and measure incremental kit sales and cost per additional patient served
Identify and approach donors or NGOs to co-fund a kit subsidy or voucher program for the lowest-income patients
Develop audio and peer-ambassador marketing materials and test in two communities before full rollout
Set a 12-month milestone of reaching 22,500 kit sales (break-even) and review whether the tiered package option becomes viable at higher volume
